adopt verb

a child

also adoption, adopted, adopted son, adopted daughter, adoptive, adoptive parents, give up for adoption, adoptive son, adoptive daughter

classical

Ter. Ad. 47: hunc majōrem adoptāvī mihi
Cic. Brut. 77: quī hunc minōrem Scīpiōnem ā Paulō adoptāvit (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 269

adoptō, adoptāre, adoptāvī, adoptātum

verb, first conjugation, transitive: aliquem (sibi fīlium) adoptāre

adopt (a child)

To take someone in the place of a son or grandson, with ab for the natural father (Lewis & Short). The parent gives a child adoptandum (Ter. Ad. 114); the adopted son is fīlius adoptīvus, and the adoption adoptiō. Its first sense is “choose” (see adopt, take up).

Other words

  • adoptiō, adoptiōnis f. — adoption

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.24: ēmancipāre fīlium alicui in adoptiōnem (Lewis & Short, as Fin. 1.7); Vell. 2.8.2: dare sē alicui in adoptiōnem (Lewis & Short)

    In Roman law the adoption of a child still in his father’s power; taking in a man already independent was arrogātiō (Lewis & Short). in adoptiōnem dare, give for adoption.

  • adoptīvus, adoptīva, adoptīvum — adopted, adoptive

    declension · also used · classical · Suet. Tib. 52 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 24: fīlius adoptīvus, fīlia adoptīva

    Of the adopted child (fīlius adoptīvus, against nātūrālis) and of the adoptive parent (pater adoptīvus, Dig.); Ovid uses it of a graft on a tree (Ars 2.652).

Examples

  • uxōrem dūxit; nātī fīliī duo: inde ego hunc majōrem adoptāvī mihi; ēdūxī ā parvulō; habuī, amāvī prō meō

    he married; two sons were born; then I adopted the elder one as my own; I brought him up from a little boy; I kept him and loved him as mineTer. Ad. 46–48

  • Tuum fīlium dedistī adoptandum mihi: is meus est factus.

    You gave me your son to adopt: he has become mine.Ter. Ad. 114–115

See also adopt, children, son, parents, childhood.

SourcesLewis & Short: adopto · Lewis & Short: adoptio · Lewis & Short: adoptivus
